steps.intent: France's objective as co-penholder alongside Greece is to secure a 12-month renewal of the Chapter VII authorization permitting maritime interdictions and inspections off the coast of Libya, providing the vital legal mandate for the European Union’s Operation IRINI to enforce the arms embargo. The primary challenge will be navigating Russian skepticism, as Moscow consistently criticizes the maritime inspection regime as unbalanced and has historically abstained or threatened to block renewals. France anticipates needing to keep the text strictly focused as a straightforward technical extension to preserve Council consensus and ensure the necessary nine affirmative votes from elected members without provoking a Russian veto.
steps.text:
The Security Council,

Recalling its resolution 1970 (2011) and all its subsequent relevant resolutions on Libya,

Recalling in particular its resolutions 2292 (2016), 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) concerning the strict implementation of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya,

Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of Libya,

Taking note of the report of the Secretary-General on the implementation of resolution 2733 (2024),

Mindful of its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security under the Charter of the United Nations,

Reaffirming that the situation in Libya continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security,

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,

1. Decides to extend the authorizations as set out in resolution 2292 (2016) and extended by resolutions 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) for a further 12 months from the date of adoption of this resolution;

2. Requests the Secretary-General to report to the Security Council on the implementation of this resolution, six months and eleven months after the adoption of this resolution;

3. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

Algeria.change: Insert a new preambular paragraph after PP2: 'Expressing deep concern that violations of the arms embargo continue unabated, particularly via land and air routes, and stressing the urgent need for a comprehensive, impartial, and balanced approach to the implementation of the arms embargo across all domains, without selectivity,'

Amend PP3 to read: 'Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity, and national unity of Libya, and stressing the importance of Libyan ownership and leadership across all political and security tracks,'

Insert a new operative paragraph after OP1: 'Demands full compliance by all Member States with the arms embargo across all domains, calls upon all Member States to cease the transfer of weapons, military equipment, and foreign fighters into Libya via land, air, and sea, and urges full cooperation with Libyan national authorities;'

China.change: Add at the end: ', and stressing that inspections on the high seas must be conducted strictly in accordance with international law, fully respecting the freedom of navigation and the legitimate rights of flag States'

Insert after 'this resolution': ', while underscoring that the arms embargo must be implemented in a comprehensive, balanced, and impartial manner across land, air, and sea routes without double standards, and that good-faith efforts to obtain the consent of the flag State must be strictly observed prior to any inspection'

Guyana.change: Insert a new preambular paragraph: 'Reiterating that the arms embargo must be fully and comprehensively implemented across all entry points, and expressing concern that the primary flows of illicit arms and related materiel into Libya continue to be transferred via land and air routes,'

Insert a new preambular paragraph: 'Reaffirming that international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982, sets out the legal framework applicable to activities in the oceans and seas, and stressing the necessity of respecting the sovereignty of flag States,'

Pakistan.change: Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of Libya, and reaffirming its support for an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process facilitated by the United Nations,

Russian Federation.change: Insert new PP: 'Underlining that the illicit transfer of arms and related materiel to and from Libya takes place across land, air, and maritime routes, and emphasizing that the arms embargo must be implemented comprehensively, impartially, and effectively across all entry points,'

Insert new PP: 'Reiterating that inspections carried out pursuant to resolution 2292 (2016) must be conducted in strict compliance with international law, including the law of the sea, with full respect for the sovereignty of flag States and without unduly delaying or hindering legitimate commercial navigation,'

Sierra Leone.change: Underscores that the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1970 (2011) should play a leading role and provide guidance on how arms and related materiel seized pursuant to the authorizations extended in paragraph 1 are disposed of, and calls upon inspecting Member States and regional organizations to coordinate closely and transparently with the Committee throughout the inspection and disposal process;

messages.Algeria: As a direct neighbor of Libya, Algeria remains deeply concerned by the continued selective focus on the maritime inspection regime, which overlooks the reality that the vast majority of illicit arms flows and external interference occur via land and air corridors. The authorizations under resolution 2292 have shown limited effectiveness while raising legitimate concerns regarding sovereignty and balance. Unless the text acknowledges the need for an impartial, comprehensive enforcement of the arms embargo across all entry routes and reaffirms genuine Libyan ownership, Algeria will maintain its position of abstention.
messages.China: China has consistently held reservations regarding the invocation of Chapter VII for high-seas vessel inspections, which must strictly respect international law, including UNCLOS, and avoid infringing upon freedom of navigation and flag-State jurisdiction. Furthermore, the enforcement of the arms embargo on Libya must be objective, balanced, and non-selective, addressing violations across land and air borders rather than focusing disproportionately on maritime routes. We urge the penholder to accommodate these concerns to help build broader consensus among Council members.
messages.Denmark: Denmark fully supports the draft resolution extending the inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) for another 12 months, which remains an essential tool for enforcing the arms embargo and preventing further destabilization in Libya. We commend France and Greece for circulating this streamlined and timely renewal, which provides vital legal authorization for maritime interdiction operations, notably EUNAVFOR MED IRINI. We favor keeping the text concise as drafted and stand ready to vote in favor.
messages.Greece: As a co-sponsor of this draft resolution alongside France, Greece fully supports the text as circulated. Renewing the authorizations under resolution 2292 is crucial for maintaining maritime stability in the Central Mediterranean and enforcing the arms embargo against illicit transfers fueling instability in Libya. We look forward to working closely with all Council members to ensure the swift and unified adoption of this essential rollover.
messages.Guyana: Guyana emphasizes that maritime interdictions under the resolution 2292 framework address only a fraction of the illicit weapon flows into Libya, while supplies by air and land borders continue largely unimpeded. To garner broader Council support, the text must reflect the need for comprehensive and impartial enforcement across all supply channels and reaffirm strict compliance with the law of the sea, including the rights of flag States. In the absence of language addressing these long-standing concerns and the effectiveness of the mechanism, Guyana will find it difficult to support the draft in its current form.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the extension of the authorizations under resolution 2292 to prevent the illicit flow of arms into Libya. We believe the arms embargo should be implemented strictly, impartially, and in full accordance with international law. In line with our principled stance, we encourage the inclusion of standard language reaffirming support for an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the draft resolution extending the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) to ensure the effective implementation of the arms embargo off the coast of Libya. Upholding international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the principle of flag State consent, remains essential to maintaining maritime security and stability in the region. We commend France and Greece for their leadership and stand ready to support the adoption of this text as drafted.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea fully supports the draft resolution extending the authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) for another 12 months. Given the fragile security environment and recent tensions in Libya, strict enforcement of the arms embargo and stemming the illicit flow of weapons by sea remain vital for regional stability. We commend France and Greece for circulating this timely and streamlined text and look forward to its swift adoption.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation maintains its principled doubts regarding the practical utility and even-handedness of the European Union's Operation IRINI, which singles out the maritime domain while turning a blind eye to land and air supply lines. Years of implementation have demonstrated that this mechanism does not stem the flow of weapons to the conflict parties and serves primarily the unilateral regional agenda of its European participants. Unless the draft reflects a truly comprehensive, balanced approach to embargo enforcement and upholds strict standards regarding flag-State consent, our delegation cannot support this mandate renewal.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone, aligned with the A3+, remains committed to the effective implementation of the arms embargo off the coast of Libya as a vital measure to de-escalate violence and protect civilians. However, as reflected in our position during the adoption of resolution 2733 (2024), it is essential that the 1970 Sanctions Committee exercise a leading role and proper oversight regarding the disposal of seized items. We urge the penholders to reflect this key priority in the text so that the Council can adopt this renewal with broader consensus.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia fully supports the draft resolution extending the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) for an additional 12 months. The arms embargo remains vital to curbing illicit arms flows and supporting stability in Libya, particularly amid recent heightened tensions. We appreciate the penholders circulating this streamlined text and stand ready to vote in favour.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft resolution extending the authorizations under resolution 2292 to uphold the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya. In light of the fragile security environment and recent clashes in Tripoli, stemming the illicit flow of weapons is crucial for Libyan stability and peace. We appreciate the penholder's streamlined text and stand ready to support its adoption.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports this draft resolution renewing the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016). Enforcing the UN arms embargo remains vital for curbing illicit arms flows into Libya and preventing further escalation, especially amid recent security tensions in Tripoli. We commend France and Greece for circulating a clean, focused renewal and look forward to its swift adoption.
messages.United States of America: The United States strongly supports the straightforward 12-month renewal of the maritime arms embargo inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) as circulated. Given the volatile security situation and continued flow of illicit weapons into Libya, preserving this vital maritime interdiction tool is essential. We commend France and Greece for keeping the text focused and clean, and we urge all Council members to support its timely adoption without weakening the mandate.

steps.summary: As co-penholder, France has preserved the core operational mandate and legal integrity of the resolution 2292 inspection authorizations for Operation IRINI while accommodating constructive, agreed language from elected members. Standard preambular text on UNCLOS, the Libyan-led political process, and general compliance across all domains was incorporated, along with an operative provision recognizing cooperation with the 1970 Committee. The draft secures a solid positive majority of at least 11 votes with no veto risk.
steps.text:
The Security Council,

Recalling its resolution 1970 (2011) and all its subsequent relevant resolutions on Libya,

Recalling in particular its resolutions 2292 (2016), 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) concerning the strict implementation of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya,

Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of Libya, and reaffirming its support for an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process facilitated by the United Nations,

Recalling that international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982, sets out the legal framework applicable to activities in the oceans and seas,

Reiterating its call on all Member States to comply fully with their obligations under resolution 1970 (2011) and all relevant subsequent resolutions concerning the arms embargo on Libya, and to cease all illicit transfers of arms and related materiel to and from Libya across all domains,

Taking note of the report of the Secretary-General on the implementation of resolution 2733 (2024),

Mindful of its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security under the Charter of the United Nations,

Reaffirming that the situation in Libya continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security,

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,

1. Decides to extend the authorizations as set out in resolution 2292 (2016) and extended by resolutions 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) for a further 12 months from the date of adoption of this resolution;

2. Welcomes the continued coordination and information-sharing between inspecting Member States and regional organizations and the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1970 (2011), and recalls the importance of continued transparency and cooperation with the Committee;

3. Requests the Secretary-General to report to the Security Council on the implementation of this resolution, six months and eleven months after the adoption of this resolution;

4. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

messages.Algeria: Algeria appreciates the penholder's incorporation of references to Libyan ownership and compliance across all domains in the preambular section. However, as an immediate neighbor directly affected by the security fallout, we must stress that monitoring maritime routes alone while illicit flows persist unimpeded across land and air domains creates an unhelpful imbalance. For the Council's action to be credible and effective, the resolution must explicitly reflect engagement with Libyan authorities and reiterate the need to address arms transfers and foreign fighters across all borders.
messages.China: China reiterates that the arms embargo on Libya must be implemented in a balanced, comprehensive, and impartial manner, avoiding selective enforcement that focuses exclusively on maritime routes while ignoring land and air violations. Furthermore, any high-seas interdiction actions must strictly respect the legitimate rights of flag States, ensure freedom of navigation, and abide by the explicit requirement to seek flag-State consent in good faith. If these legitimate and longstanding concerns are not accommodated in the text, China will not be in a position to support the draft resolution.
messages.Denmark: Denmark fully supports the draft resolution as presented by France and co-sponsored by Greece. Effective enforcement of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya is vital for de-escalating tensions, supporting a Libyan-led political process, and upholding international law, including UNCLOS. We look forward to voting in favour of this text.
messages.Greece: As a proud co-sponsor of this draft resolution alongside France, Greece fully supports the current text in Revision 1. The renewal of the mandate established under resolution 2292 is essential to enforcing the arms embargo, countering illicit weapons flows, and maintaining maritime security in the Central Mediterranean in full accordance with international law, including UNCLOS. We look forward to its swift and unanimous adoption by the Security Council.
messages.Guyana: Guyana appreciates the co-penholders' constructive engagement and the inclusion of language referencing all domains and UNCLOS. However, as documented extensively by the Panel of Experts, the overwhelming majority of illicit arms flows into Libya bypass maritime routes and enter via land and air. Explicitly reflecting this reality is critical for ensuring a comprehensive and non-selective implementation of the arms embargo and will be an important factor in determining Guyana's final vote.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan thanks the penholder for accommodating our proposal in preambular paragraph 3, which appropriately underlines the importance of an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process. We remain committed to Libya's sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity, and national unity, as well as the full implementation of the arms embargo. Pakistan is satisfied with the current text of the draft resolution and stands ready to vote in favour.
messages.Panama: Panama fully supports the draft resolution renewing the authorization under resolution 2292 (2016) to enforce the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya. We welcome the explicit reference to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea as the legal framework governing maritime activities, as well as the text's focus on transparency and coordination with the Sanctions Committee. We are prepared to vote in favour of the text as currently drafted.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea fully supports the draft resolution renewing the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) for another 12 months. We commend France and Greece for their balanced, streamlined text, which is vital for enforcing the arms embargo, enhancing maritime security, and supporting stability in Libya. We stand ready to vote in favour of the resolution as drafted.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation maintains serious doubts regarding the practical effectiveness and impartiality of maritime interdiction mechanisms off the coast of Libya, which disproportionately focus on the sea while illicit arms deliveries persist via land and air borders. While we take note of the penholder's modest adjustments, the text continues to cater primarily to the unilateral interests of the European Union's Operation IRINI. Without a truly balanced and comprehensive approach addressing all channels of illicit supplies and ensuring strict respect for flag State rights, we cannot support this resolution and intend to abstain.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone appreciates the penholders' inclusion of operative paragraph 2 acknowledging coordination and transparency with the 1970 Sanctions Committee. However, as consistently highlighted by our delegation and our African partners, clear reference to coordination with the Committee regarding the disposal of seized materiel is crucial. Incorporating explicit reference to the disposal process into OP2 will enable Sierra Leone to fully support the text.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia fully supports the draft resolution as presented by France and Greece, renewing the authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) for another 12 months. Upholding the arms embargo and maritime inspection regime, in full accordance with international law including UNCLOS, is essential to curbing illicit arms flows and supporting stability in Libya. We appreciate the penholders' efforts and stand ready to vote in favour of the text.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft resolution renewing the maritime inspection authorizations off the coast of Libya to curb illicit arms flows. Strict adherence to the arms embargo and the preservation of Libya's sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity remain paramount. We appreciate the penholder's efforts to keep the text focused and effective, and we stand ready to vote in favour.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom fully supports the draft resolution renewing the maritime arms embargo authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016). Strict enforcement of the arms embargo remains essential to preventing further destabilization and supporting the UN-facilitated political process in Libya. We thank France and Greece for circulating a clean, balanced text and stand ready to vote in favour.
messages.United States of America: The United States strongly supports the draft resolution extending the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 for an additional 12 months. Enforcing the arms embargo and stemming the illicit flow of weapons into Libya is essential to regional stability and to supporting an inclusive, Libyan-led political process. We commend France and Greece for preparing a balanced, straightforward text and stand ready to vote in favor.

steps.summary: France, as penholder alongside Greece, accommodated key proposals from China, Algeria, Guyana, and Sierra Leone regarding arms flows across land and air domains, flag-State consent, disposal of seized materiel, and engagement with Libyan authorities. These additions uphold the core mandate of resolution 2292 and European maritime operations under international law while ensuring broad Council support, with only the Russian Federation expected to abstain.

The Security Council,

Recalling its resolution 1970 (2011) and all its subsequent relevant resolutions on Libya,

Recalling in particular its resolutions 2292 (2016), 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) concerning the strict implementation of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya,

reasons.Algeria: Algeria voted in favour because the penholder fully accommodated our key concerns and text proposals, specifically including explicit references to Libyan national authorities and addressing illicit arms transfers and mercenary flows across land and air borders.
reasons.China: China's proposed amendments regarding strict and impartial implementation across all domains (land, air, and sea) and reminding inspecting entities to respect flag-State consent and international law were fully incorporated by the co-sponsors, allowing China to vote in favour while reserving any explanation of vote for after the adoption.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark consistently supports the enforcement of the UN arms embargo on Libya, maritime security under UNCLOS, and the renewal of the inspection mandate under resolution 2292. As an EU member state aligned with the penholders, we vote in favour without needing to deliver a statement prior to the vote.
reasons.France: As the penholder and author of the draft resolution renewing the maritime arms embargo inspections authorization off the coast of Libya (Operation IRINI), France strongly supports the adoption of the text.
reasons.Greece: As a co-sponsor of the draft resolution and an EU member state directly invested in Mediterranean maritime security and Operation IRINI, Greece unequivocally votes in favour of renewing the resolution 2292 framework. Delivering a brief statement before the vote reinforces Greece's active role as co-penholder/sponsor and highlights its commitment to UNCLOS and arms embargo compliance.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana voted in favour after its proposed amendment stressing the need to address illicit arms flows across all domains—particularly land and air routes—was fully accepted and incorporated by the penholders into the final text.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the renewal of authorizations under resolution 2292 to uphold the arms embargo and promote stability in Libya, particularly as our core concerns regarding Libyan sovereignty and the UN-facilitated, Libyan-led political process have been reflected in the text.
reasons.Panama: Panama supports the renewal of the maritime arms embargo inspections authorization under resolution 2292, particularly as the text preserves key principles of international law, including the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the requirement of good-faith efforts to obtain flag State consent.
reasons.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea consistently supports the strict implementation of the arms embargo on Libya, including the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) and its successor resolutions, to curb illicit arms flows and promote stability. In line with our previous vote in favour of resolution 2733 (2024) and our position during consultations, we vote in favour of the draft resolution.
reasons.Russian Federation: Consistent with our established position on the renewal of the high-seas inspection mandate under resolution 2292 (most recently resolutions 2684 and 2733), Russia abstains due to the European Union's biased and ineffective implementation via Operation IRINI, which ignores illicit arms flows via land and air and fails to uphold strict impartiality.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Our primary concern from the 2024 renewal regarding the role of the 1970 Sanctions Committee in the inspection and disposal process of seized materiel has been successfully accommodated by the co-sponsors in operative paragraph 3. As our key proposals on transparency, coordination, and the Committee's oversight role have been integrated into the draft text, Sierra Leone votes in favour and reserves its remarks for after the vote.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia steadfastly supports the renewal of the maritime arms embargo interdiction mandate off the coast of Libya, which is essential for regional stability and aligns fully with our European Union commitments and past voting record on resolution 2733.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia supports the extension of the maritime inspection mandate under resolution 2292 to curb illicit arms flows, maintain the ceasefire, and support Libya's stability and sovereignty, consistent with our previous votes and our position during negotiations.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom consistently supports the renewal of the maritime arms embargo inspections mandate under resolution 2292 (2016) to curb illicit weapons flows into Libya, aligning fully with our longstanding policy and close coordination with European partners.
reasons.United States of America: The United States strongly supports extending the maritime inspection authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) to curb illicit arms flows and enforce the UN arms embargo in Libya. As is standard practice for this recurring mandate renewal, the delegation will cast an affirmative vote and reserve any remarks for an explanation of vote following the adoption.

steps.text:
The Security Council,

Recalling its resolution 1970 (2011) and all its subsequent relevant resolutions on Libya,

Recalling in particular its resolutions 2292 (2016), 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) concerning the strict implementation of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya,

Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of Libya, and reaffirming its support for an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process facilitated by the United Nations,

Recalling that international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982, sets out the legal framework applicable to activities in the oceans and seas,

Reiterating its call on all Member States to comply fully with their obligations under resolution 1970 (2011) and all relevant subsequent resolutions concerning the arms embargo on Libya, and to cease all illicit transfers of arms and related materiel to and from Libya across all domains, particularly via land and air routes where the primary flows of illicit arms are reported to occur,

Taking note of the report of the Secretary-General on the implementation of resolution 2733 (2024),

Mindful of its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security under the Charter of the United Nations,

Reaffirming that the situation in Libya continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security,

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,

1. Decides to extend the authorizations as set out in resolution 2292 (2016) and extended by resolutions 2357 (2017), 2420 (2018), 2473 (2019), 2526 (2020), 2578 (2021), 2635 (2022), 2684 (2023) and 2733 (2024) for a further 12 months from the date of adoption of this resolution, and underscores that the arms embargo must be implemented strictly, impartially, and comprehensively across all domains, including land, air, and sea;

2. Urges Member States to respect and support the full implementation of the 23 October 2020 ceasefire agreement, including by preventing the illicit transfer of arms, materiel, and foreign fighters and mercenaries into Libya across all domains, notably through air and land borders;

3. Welcomes the continued coordination and information-sharing between inspecting Member States and regional organizations and the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1970 (2011), recalls the importance of continued transparency and cooperation with the Committee throughout the inspection and disposal process, underscores the need for close coordination with the Committee regarding the disposal of seized arms and related materiel, encourages enhanced consultation and cooperation with the relevant Libyan authorities, and reminds inspecting Member States and regional organizations of the requirement to make good-faith efforts to obtain the consent of the vessel's flag State prior to any inspection and to conduct inspections strictly within the authorized scope and international law;

4. Requests the Secretary-General to report to the Security Council on the implementation of this resolution, six months and eleven months after the adoption of this resolution;

5. Decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

before.France:
France, together with Greece, is honoured to submit to the Council the draft resolution renewing for twelve months the authorizations granted under resolution 2292 (2016) regarding the inspection of vessels on the high seas off the coast of Libya.

The strict implementation of the arms embargo remains essential to supporting the stability of Libya, preserving the 23 October 2020 ceasefire agreement, and creating the necessary conditions for a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political settlement. Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI plays an indispensable, impartial, and transparent role in deterring illicit arms flows in the maritime domain, in full compliance with international law and the Law of the Sea.

In light of the persistent security challenges and recent tensions in Libya, maintaining this mechanism is vital. We thank all Council members for their constructive engagement throughout the negotiations, and we urge all delegations to vote in favour of this draft resolution.
before.Greece:
Mr. President,

Greece has co-sponsored the draft resolution before us today, and we strongly urge all Council members to vote in its favour.

The renewal of the authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) remains an indispensable tool in our collective efforts to enforce the United Nations arms embargo on Libya and prevent the illicit flow of weapons that continues to threaten the country’s stability and the wider Mediterranean region. 

As a Mediterranean state committed to international law, in particular the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), Greece underlines the crucial role of maritime security operations, including the European Union’s Operation IRINI, which act strictly, impartially, and in accordance with international law to implement the Council's mandate.

At a time of heightened fragility on the ground in Libya, upholding the arms embargo across all domains and supporting the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process are vital. We thank France for its leadership as penholder and look forward to the adoption of this resolution.

Thank you.

after.Algeria:
Mr. President,

Algeria voted in favour of the resolution just adopted renewing the authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016).

Allow me at the outset to thank the co-penholders, France and Greece, for their constructive engagement throughout the negotiations and for taking into account key concerns raised during the consultations. 

For Algeria, as an immediate neighbour bound to Libya by profound historical, cultural, and fraternal ties, the stability, sovereignty, and unity of Libya are of paramount importance. Our support for this resolution is guided by our principled commitment to preserving the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national unity of Libya.

Algeria has consistently underscored that the arms embargo must not be implemented selectively. The reports of the Panel of Experts and the Secretary-General have repeatedly demonstrated that the primary illicit flows of weapons, military equipment, and foreign fighters enter Libya not primarily by sea, but rather through land and air routes. We welcome that the resolution adopted today explicitly recognizes this reality and underscores that the arms embargo must be implemented strictly, impartially, and comprehensively across all domains—land, air, and sea alike. 

Furthermore, we stress that any inspection activities conducted on the high seas must strictly adhere to international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and fully respect the sovereignty of flag States, including the requirement to make good-faith efforts to obtain flag-State consent prior to any inspection. Close consultation and coordination with the relevant Libyan authorities and the 1970 Sanctions Committee remain essential throughout this process.

Enforcing the arms embargo is an integral part of supporting the 23 October 2020 ceasefire agreement. In this regard, Algeria reiterates its call for the immediate, complete, and unconditional withdrawal of all foreign forces, foreign fighters, and mercenaries from all Libyan territory.

Finally, Algeria reaffirms that there can be no military solution to the Libyan crisis. Lasting peace and stability can only be achieved through an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process, facilitated by the United Nations, leading to the holding of free, fair, and transparent national presidential and legislative elections, and fulfilling the legitimate aspirations of the brotherly Libyan people. Algeria will continue to stand firmly alongside our Libyan brothers and sisters to support national reconciliation and achieve enduring peace and prosperity.

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Russian Federation:
(spoke in Russian):

The Russian Federation abstained in the voting on the draft resolution submitted by France and Greece renewing the authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016).

Our principled position regarding the European Union’s maritime Operation IRINI on the high seas off the coast of Libya remains well known and unchanged. Over the years of its existence, this operation has demonstrated an extremely low level of practical effectiveness. As the reports of the United Nations Panel of Experts have repeatedly confirmed, the primary flows of illicit arms and materiel into Libya continue to be carried out via land and air corridors, over which Operation IRINI has neither reach nor jurisdiction. 

Furthermore, serious questions persist regarding the selectivity and transparency of the operation’s activities, as well as the need for strict compliance with the norms of international law, including the Law of the Sea, and the requirement to obtain the consent of flag States prior to inspections. We have repeatedly witnessed how the European Union uses Security Council mandates under Chapter VII of the Charter to advance its own regional geopolitical and security interests rather than genuinely addressing the needs of the Libyan people.

The protracted crisis, security vacuum, and deep political division that Libya faces to this day are the direct consequence of the blatant aggression committed by NATO in 2011, which shattered Libyan statehood. Overcoming these dire consequences requires comprehensive, impartial, and balanced international assistance that strictly respects the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Libya, rather than half-measures that do not produce tangible results on the ground.
after.Sierra Leone:
Mr. President,

I have the honour to deliver this explanation of vote on behalf of the three African members of the Security Council—Algeria, Somalia, and Sierra Leone—as well as Guyana (A3+).

The A3+ voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, which renews for a period of twelve months the authorizations provided under resolution 2292 (2016). We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national unity of Libya, as well as our support for an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process facilitated by the United Nations.

The strict and impartial enforcement of the arms embargo on Libya is vital to de-escalating violence, ensuring civilian protection, and creating conditions conducive to a lasting political settlement. Today, our delegations cast an affirmative vote because our core concerns and key proposals have been meaningfully reflected in the adopted text.

In particular, the A3+ welcomes the resolution's explicit recognition that the arms embargo must be implemented comprehensively across all domains—sea, air, and land. As consistently highlighted by reports of the Panel of Experts, the predominant flows of illicit weapons and materiel into Libya do not occur via maritime routes, but rather through porous land borders and air corridors. Addressing maritime trafficking while neglecting land and air routes risks creating an imbalance in enforcement. We therefore appreciate the inclusion of clear language underscoring the urgent need to halt illicit transfers across all borders and domains.

Furthermore, we welcome the emphasis placed on close coordination and transparency with the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1970 (2011), particularly regarding the disposal of seized arms and related materiel. We also value the call for enhanced consultation and cooperation with the relevant Libyan authorities and the reaffirmation of the requirement to strictly respect the provisions of international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and to make good-faith efforts to obtain the consent of flag States prior to inspections.

The A3+ reiterates its call for the full implementation of the 23 October 2020 ceasefire agreement, including the immediate withdrawal of all foreign fighters, foreign forces, and mercenaries from Libya. We urge all international actors and Member States to refrain from any actions that exacerbate divisions or fuel the conflict, and to direct their collective efforts toward supporting the aspirations of the Libyan people for peace, reconciliation, and the holding of free and fair national elections.

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Slovenia:
Mr. President,

Slovenia welcomes the adoption of today’s resolution renewing the authorizations under resolution 2292 (2016) for an additional twelve months. We thank the co-sponsors, France and Greece, for their dedicated efforts throughout the negotiations to reach a text that garnered such overwhelming support.

The effective, comprehensive, and impartial implementation of the arms embargo on Libya remains vital for de-escalating tensions, safeguarding the 2020 ceasefire agreement, and creating the necessary space for an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process facilitated by the United Nations. 

In this regard, we commend the European Union’s Operation IRINI for its indispensable and professional contribution to maritime security off the coast of Libya. Operating in strict accordance with the Council's mandate, international law, and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Operation IRINI plays a crucial and transparent role in deterring illicit arms transfers and contributing to broader regional stability.

At the same time, we underline that the arms embargo must be respected across all domains. Illicit transfers of weapons and military equipment by land and air continue to fuel instability and undermine peace efforts. We reiterate our call on all Member States to fully comply with their obligations under resolution 1970 (2011) and subsequent resolutions, to cease any foreign interference, and to support the immediate and complete withdrawal of all foreign forces, foreign fighters, and mercenaries from Libyan soil.

Only a unified, stable Libya, with legitimate and reunified state institutions, can ensure lasting peace and prosperity for the Libyan people. Slovenia remains fully committed to supporting Libya and the efforts of UNSMIL on this path.

Thank you.
after.United States of America:
Thank you, Mr. President.

The United States voted in favour of this resolution, and we thank the co-penholders, France and Greece, for their dedicated leadership and constructive engagement throughout this process.

The reauthorization of the maritime interdiction mandate under resolution 2292 (2016) remains a vital component of the international community's efforts to enforce the United Nations arms embargo on Libya. Operation IRINI plays a critical, impartial role in deterring illicit maritime weapons transfers and enhancing transparency, strictly in accordance with international law.

However, as the Panel of Experts has repeatedly documented, the vast majority of weapons, ammunition, and foreign materiel entering Libya continue to arrive by land and air routes. Strict implementation of the arms embargo cannot be confined to the high seas alone. We urge all Member States to uphold their obligations under resolution 1970 (2011) and cease all illicit arms transfers across every domain.

The recent outbreak of armed clashes in Tripoli underscores just how fragile the security situation in Libya remains. Lasting stability will remain out of reach so long as external actors fuel division, funnel weapons, and maintain foreign forces, fighters, and mercenaries on Libyan soil. We reiterate our call for the immediate, unconditional, and complete withdrawal of all foreign forces, fighters, and mercenaries from Libya, in full accordance with the 23 October 2020 ceasefire agreement.

The United States reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national unity of Libya. We will continue to support the Libyan people and the United Nations Support Mission in Libya in advancing an inclusive, Libyan-led and Libyan-owned political process that can lead to free, fair, and credible national elections and the reunification of the country's military and civil institutions.

Thank you, Mr. President.
